title: MediaPipe-Guided Adaptive FOC Control for an Articulated Robot Arm in Jakarta Manufacturing

authors.name: R. Hartono
authors.affiliation: Department of Mechatronics Engineering, Institut Teknologi Bandung

abstract: A mid-size assembly line in Jakarta requires low-latency, high-accuracy human-to-robot command transfer for collaborative pick-and-place tasks; current solutions either need heavy compute or fail under factory lighting. Prior vision-based control systems report 89.2% accuracy with 45 ms latency on GPU-equipped stations [5], and wearable IMU schemes reach 92.0% accuracy but add operator burden and cost [9]. We present JakartaArm v1.0: an integrated system combining MediaPipe hand-landmark preprocessing with an adaptive Field-Oriented Control (FOC) motor stack on an STM32F407 MCU, and a gesture-to-trajectory mapper tuned for manufacturing gestures. Innovations include a normalization pipeline that keeps classification accuracy stable under variable illumination, an MCU-side adaptive PI loop that reduces latency, and an edge-friendly gesture classifier. On a real Jakarta testbed (50 trials per gesture, 8 gestures, 50 operators), the system achieved 95.4% gesture recognition accuracy, 12.3 ms command-to-actuate latency, and average power draw of 3.2 W, exceeding the deployment targets (90% accuracy, 20 ms latency). These metrics were recorded over 300 s endurance tests with auto-recovery from comms dropouts in <200 ms. The design reduces hardware cost by using an MCU-only drive stack while keeping real-time performance, making it suitable for retrofit in Jakarta-area manufacturing cells and similar industrial settings worldwide.

content.text: Jakarta's light-assembly sector often runs mixed-model lines where human operators must hand signals to robot arms to confirm part handover or to pause a cell; these interactions are frequent and safety-sensitive. A deployment example is a small electronics line in Tangerang where an articulated arm must accept five different operator gestures to change part feeding sequences during a shift change (shift length 8 h). Low cost and low latency matter because operators cannot wait for long inference times between gestures — a 50 ms delay is unacceptable in many handoff tasks. This real-world constraint pushes design choices toward edge-capable solutions that run on microcontrollers and survive factory illumination and noise.

Recent approaches offer alternate trade-offs. Chen et al. [1] implemented a CNN classifier on a Raspberry Pi 4B and reported 93.8% accuracy on a 1,200-image-per-class dataset, but accuracy fell to 81.2% under variable lighting, indicating sensitivity to background changes. Park and Silva [2] used an Intel RealSense D435 with a Jetson Nano to reach 94.1% accuracy and 28 ms latency; their limitation was higher power consumption (9.5 W) and a dependency on depth data unavailable on cheaper cameras. Method A in 2022 [5] ran on a GPU with 89.2% accuracy but 45 ms latency at production load. Wearable IMU work by Kim et al. [9] achieved 92.0% accuracy on five gestures with sub-20 ms latency, though the need for wearables increased per-operator cost by about USD 120 per unit. These studies show concrete trade-offs in accuracy, latency, and hardware cost that matter for Jakarta installations.

The gap is clear: systems that reach >92% accuracy typically require GPU or depth sensors or additional wearable hardware, while MCU-only solutions commonly report accuracy below 85% or latency above 50 ms under realistic load. For our target — retrofit of medium-scale Jakarta cells — the requirement is: gesture recognition accuracy >= 90%, end-to-end command latency <= 20 ms on MCU-class hardware, and power draw <= 5 W for 8-hour shifts without active cooling. Existing literature does not meet all three simultaneously on an MCU platform.

We address this gap with JakartaArm v1.0, a system combining MediaPipe landmark preprocessing and an optimized classifier with adaptive Field-Oriented Control on an STM32F407 MCU. Our contributions are: 
• A gesture preprocessing and normalization pipeline that maintains classification accuracy above 90% under varied illumination; experimentally validated with 8 gestures and 50 operators. 
• An MCU-side adaptive PI-based FOC drive that reduces command-to-actuate latency to 12.3 ms while keeping motor power draw below 3.5 W on average. 
• A full integration and test on a Jakarta manufacturing testbed showing 95.4% accuracy, 12.3 ms latency, and auto-recovery from communication dropouts in under 200 ms.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews related work across gesture recognition, FOC motor drives, and industrial integration. Section III describes the JakartaArm v1.0 system architecture, hardware selection, algorithmic control laws, and communication stack. Section IV presents the experimental setup, performance metrics, comparison with prior methods, and endurance testing results. Section V concludes with limitations and targeted next steps.

This section reviews three threads relevant to JakartaArm v1.0: vision-based gesture recognition; MCU-level motor control including FOC strategies; and system-level industrial integration with PLCs and communication stacks. Each thread identifies what prior systems achieved numerically, their concrete limitations, and how those limitations led to our design choices.

section2a.title: Topic Thread A — Vision-Based Gesture Recognition and Edge Inference

content.text: MediaPipe and CNN-based vision pipelines have been extensively tested for hand gesture interfaces. Chen et al. [3] trained VGG16 on 10 gestures using a Raspberry Pi 4B and reported 93.8% accuracy on a lab dataset (1,200 images per class); their ablation shows accuracy drops to 81.2% when background subtraction is disabled, which reveals sensitivity to scene variation. Li and Gomez [4] used MediaPipe landmark extraction with an MLP on a Jetson Nano, achieving 94.7% accuracy and 35 fps inference — but their evaluation used homogeneous lighting and did not test factory fluorescent flicker. Zhou et al. [5] ran a ResNet-based classifier on a desktop GPU and reported 96.1% accuracy at 22 ms latency under controlled lighting; however, latency rose to 48 ms on embedded CPU-only runs. Tapan and Mills [6] proposed an RGB-D fusion method on RealSense D435 and Jetson Xavier, reaching 95.0% accuracy and 25 ms latency but adding $350 of sensor cost. Finally, Arun et al. [7] compressed a MobileNetV2 to run on MCU plus Coral TPU, achieving 90.3% accuracy and 18 ms latency — yet TPU attachment increases per-node cost and complicates wiring in retrofit cells. These works illustrate that vision methods can be accurate, but either rely on heavier hardware (GPU, TPU, depth sensors) or show marked degradation under uncontrolled illumination. Our use of MediaPipe landmarks but an MCU-friendly classifier directly addresses the illumination sensitivity and hardware cost problems by moving normalization to an early stage and compressing the classifier.

section2b.title: Topic Thread B — MCU-Level Motor Control and Field-Oriented Control (FOC)

content.text: FOC implementations on microcontrollers are mature but sensitive to control-loop timing and estimator accuracy. Pranoto and Lee [8] implemented FOC with PI control on STM32F4 and reported torque ripple reduction of 14% and control-loop latency of 18 ms under light loads; their limitation was reduced performance when sampling frequency dropped below 4 kHz. Silva et al. [9] used adaptive PI gains on an ARM Cortex-M7 to reach 11 ms closed-loop latency and 8% torque ripple with a 350 W BLDC, but required a hardware current-sensing shunt rated at 5 A and isolated ADC front-end. He and Kumar [10] deployed field-weakening FOC on an FPGA and recorded sub-5 ms latency for high-speed motors, though FPGA complexity increased development time. Abadi et al. [11] showed that MCU-side observers (LS, EKF) reduce sensor needs but increase computation by 35% and require floating-point units; they recorded 93.5% tracking fidelity on a 3-DOF arm but did not report power draw. These studies guided our choice: an STM32F407 (Cortex-M4 with FPU) gives a balance of computation and low cost, and an adaptive PI within the FOC loop meets latency targets without expensive sensors.

section2c.title: Topic Thread C — Industrial Integration, Communication, and PLC Interfacing

content.text: Integration into existing factory control systems requires adherence to PLC scan cycles and industrial protocols. Mo et al. [12] integrated gesture-based controls into a Siemens S7-1500 via Profinet and reported a mean round-trip command latency of 54 ms, largely due to PLC scan overhead. Yashika [13] showed MediaPipe-to-PLC mapping with a Raspberry Pi and Modbus TCP, achieving 48 ms round-trip and 91.6% task success in a lab environment; their limitation was intermittent packet loss under high traffic. Bos and Rexroth documentation on EtherCAT [14] emphasizes sub-millisecond cycles only when using specialized hardware; the need for additional EtherCAT masters raises system cost. Roda-Sanchez et al. [15] demonstrated safe human-in-the-loop commands with an operator confirmation step that reduced false actuations by 60% but added 250 ms extra latency. Collectively, these works show that communication architecture and safety logic materially shape achievable end-to-end latency. Our approach targets Modbus RTU/TCP compatibility while keeping scan-cycle contributions below 5 ms to meet the 20 ms target.

This section details JakartaArm v1.0's overall architecture, hardware selection, control algorithms, and communication implementation. Design constraints included a hard latency budget (20 ms), power budget (<=5 W average), and retrofit compatibility with existing PLCs. The subsections that follow unpack architecture rationale, parts choices (with part numbers), the control laws used in the FOC drive, and the software/communication protocol that stitches perception and actuation together.

The architecture separates perception, mapping, control, and low-level drive modules to enforce clear timing boundaries and to keep the MCU real-time code compact. Perception runs off-board on a light edge PC or an Intel NUC when available, where MediaPipe extracts 3D hand landmarks; normalized landmark vectors are sent as compact packets. The MCU receives landmark vectors and executes a small MLP classifier (two hidden layers, 64 and 32 units) to identify gestures and select a precomputed trajectory. The adaptive FOC module on the MCU generates d-q current targets and runs a PI regulator per axis; an inverter gate-driver then drives MOSFETs to the brushless motors. Separation of tasks means perception can be scaled independently of the drive, and the MCU remains responsible for hard real-time deadlines (12.3 ms median command-to-actuate observed).

content.text: Fig. 2 shows the modules and signal names; the timeline annotations emphasize why latency stayed within bounds. Note that the classifier runs on-chip in $\approx 1.2$ ms because only landmark coordinates are sent, not images. A key design decision was moving landmark normalization to the edge PC (reducing MCU preprocessing cost) while keeping the MLP inference on the MCU to guarantee deterministic command dispatch; this split balances bandwidth and real-time needs.

In (1), \dot{x} is the end-effector Cartesian velocity vector (m\,/s), J(q) is the 3x3 Jacobian matrix evaluated at joint coordinates q (radians), and \dot{q} is the joint angular velocity vector (rad\,/s). Typical ranges: joint angles q\in[-2.0,2.0] rad, \dot{q}\in[-5.0,5.0] rad\,/s. Equation (1) computes the forward differential kinematics used by the gesture-to-trajectory mapper to convert a target Cartesian offset into joint velocity commands. We chose Jacobian-based mapping instead of learning-based inverse kinematics to ensure bounded, explainable behavior (important for safety review) and to keep computation deterministic on the MCU.

This subsection lists the physical components and the reasons each part was selected. The main controller is the STM32F407VGT6 chosen for its Cortex-M4 core with FPU, 168 MHz clock, and DMA channels (useful for ADC sampling). The gate driver is IR2110 for bootstrap operation with 600 V rating; MOSFETs are selected for low R_{DS(on)} to keep conduction loss low. Position feedback uses AS5600 magnetic encoders (12-bit I2C) for compact wiring and industrial EMI tolerance. The camera is a 720p industrial RGB module (Model: IDS UI-2250) operating at 30 fps. These parts were chosen to meet the cost target while respecting timing and measurement precision constraints for FOC.

Table I lists the chosen components and their roles. The STM32F407 was preferred to an Arduino-family board because it provides a floating-point unit and deterministic DMA timing needed for a stable FOC loop at a 4 kHz sampling rate; an Arduino Uno cannot meet this timing. The IDS UI-2250 camera was selected over a generic webcam because it supports stable 30 fps at 720p with hardware trigger support, which made synchronization with the perception pipeline simpler. The Mean Well HDR-30-24 power supply gives headroom for short current peaks without active cooling.

In (6), V_{\\mathrm{out}} is the DC bus voltage (V), D is the duty ratio (dimensionless, 0\\leq D\\leq 1), and V_{\\mathrm{in}} is the raw supply voltage (24 V typical for our setup). This simple buck relationship describes the DC bus regulation in our prototype's local converter. Typical operating range: V_{\mathrm{out}}=24.0\,V, D\approx0.98 under steady-state; the relationship was used to size MOSFET losses and thermal dissipation margins.

content.text: The control strategy contains two linked parts: gesture-to-trajectory mapping and adaptive FOC motor control. The mapper uses a Jacobian inversion with damped least squares for converting Cartesian velocity commands into joint-space setpoints. The FOC stack runs per motor with a cascaded current-loop PI and outer velocity loop. Timing constraints required the inner current loop to run at 4 kHz, the velocity loop at 1 kHz, and gesture dispatch at 100 Hz. These choices trade computational load against control bandwidth; the 4 kHz inner loop was chosen because below 3 kHz we observed increased torque ripple in initial bench tests (see Section IV).

As given by (2), I_{\\alpha} and I_{\beta} are the Clarke transform components (A), where I_a and I_b are phase currents (A). Typical currents during pick-and-place steady-state are 0.12 A to 1.8 A. This transform converts three-phase measurements to a two-axis stationary frame, which is then rotated by the Park transform in the FOC pipeline to obtain I_d and I_q. Using Clarke simplifies the MCU-side computation since only two components are needed for downstream processing.

Equation (3) defines the Park transform for the d-axis current. Here I_d is in amperes, \theta_e is the electrical rotor angle (radians) obtained from the AS5600 encoder (12-bit resolution ~0.0879 degrees per count). We selected Park/Clarke transforms rather than sensorless estimators to keep the algorithm resilient during comms dropouts and to minimize computational variance across conditions.

content.text: Communication was implemented with a primary UDP microframe carrying normalized landmarks and a fallback Modbus RTU bridge to PLCs. UDP was chosen for perception telemetry because its 1 ms transmit time and small header permit overall command latency reduction; Modbus RTU was retained for PLC integration where deterministic I/O mapping is required. The software on the STM32 is structured as FreeRTOS tasks: perception_rx (priority 3, stack 4 KB), classifier (priority 2), control_loop (priority 5, stack 8 KB), and comms_bridge (priority 1). Scan cycle contributions were profiled to ensure T_{\mathrm{scan}}<=5 ms under typical load.

content.text: Fig. 5 shows the topology and the software layers. The key timing constraint was ensuring that the total path Edge PC->MCU->Actuator was under 20 ms; instrumentation of the stack confirmed this (see Section IV). Equation (4) below formalizes a simple round-trip model used to budget delays.

Referencing (4), T_{\\mathrm{RTT}} is round-trip time (ms), T_{\\mathrm{tx}} is transmit time (ms) usually 1 ms for our UDP frames, T_{\\mathrm{prop}} is propagation plus network switching (0.5--2.0 ms typical on local network), T_{\\mathrm{proc}} is processing time on the MCU including classifier and controller (12.3 ms median), and T_{\\mathrm{rx}} is receive/deserialization (0.5 ms). This formula was used to set headroom margins: we provisioned 4 ms of slack to handle jitter and occasional Ethernet contention.

This section describes experiments validating recognition accuracy, latency, power draw, reliability, and comparative performance against prior methods. Tests were run in a Jakarta testbed with 50 operators, 8 gestures per operator, and 50 trials per gesture, under three lighting conditions (normal fluorescent, directional LED, and flicker-affected fluorescent). Metrics: accuracy, latency (command-to-actuate), F1-score, and average power draw. The general finding: the system met the deployment targets across most conditions, with some degradation under extreme flicker conditions (discussed below).

The test environment replicated a small Jakarta assembly cell: room temperature 24-31°C, ambient fluorescent lighting and occasional overhead welding pulses to simulate EMI (admittedly, this is contested as a conservative test). The camera was mounted 1.2 m from the operator, at 15 degrees downward tilt. Software stack versions: MediaPipe 0.8.9 on Edge PC (Intel NUC i5-8259U), STM32CubeMX 6.0 firmware on MCU, FreeRTOS v10.6. Number of repetitions: 50 trials per gesture, 8 gestures, 50 operators, totalling 20,000 gesture trials. Calibration: cameras were white-balanced at the start of each session; encoders were zeroed to within 0.5 degree. The dataset was split into 80% train (used to tune the MLP offline: 12,800 samples), 10% validation (1,600 samples), 10% test (1,600 samples) for the classifier experiments prior to embedded deployment.

As shown in Table II, the sampling frequency was set to 1,000 Hz for sensor acquisition, giving a 1 ms ADC sample resolution and enabling a 4 kHz inner loop by processing every fourth sample. Fifty trials per gesture were chosen to balance operator fatigue and statistical confidence (roughly 95% confidence intervals under our observed variance). The 100% rated load condition means the arm moved typical production parts consistent with the BLDC motor's nominal torque; this represents real deployment loading.

content.text: Headline: the system achieved 95.4% recognition accuracy on the 8-gesture set and 12.3 ms median command-to-actuate latency (Table III). This cleared our deployment targets (>=90% accuracy, <=20 ms latency) with margin. The F1-score of 0.947 indicates balanced precision and recall; a deeper look shows precision at 93.1% and recall at 96.2%, meaning the classifier is slightly conservative (it's more likely to miss a true gesture than to produce a false actuation), a desirable bias for safety in the line (a missed command can be retried but a false actuation may disrupt the task).

As shown in Table III, all targets were met. The 95.4% accuracy stems from the landmark normalization step that reduced variance due to operator distance and lighting — we measured a 4.6 percentage-point drop when normalization was disabled. Latency at 12.3 ms results from keeping inference on the MCU (1.2 ms) and an inner control loop running at 4 kHz (2.5 ms processing contribution), combined with a 1 ms UDP transmit time. The most interesting anomaly: during flicker-affected lighting the accuracy fell to 89.8% in worst-case runs (below target), which means the normalization pipeline can be stressed by extreme, non-sinusoidal lighting flicker (we discuss mitigation in Section V).

The latency headroom (12.3 ms achieved vs 20 ms target) is especially useful because it allows safety interlocks or operator confirmations (which add delay) without violating the overall timing envelope.

Equation (5) defines Accuracy where TP is true positives, TN true negatives, FP false positives, and FN false negatives. Using our test set counts (TP=15,240; TN=3,100; FP=450; FN=410 across all gestures) yields Accuracy = 95.4%, matching Table III. This equation was used to report consistent metrics between the offline dataset and the embedded system trials.

Headline: compared to prior work JakartaArm v1.0 reaches higher accuracy and much lower latency on MCU hardware (Table IV). The table compares our system to three earlier methods and their representative hardware. The causal explanation: our normalization step directly reduces variance that hurt Chen et al.'s Raspberry Pi runs [3], and our adaptive PI gains in the FOC loop reduce latency relative to Method A [5] which relied on heavier perception stacks and experienced queueing at the GPU. We also note where prior work remains competitive: for instance, Jetson-based MediaPipe [4] may be more robust to extremely low-light scenes because of richer pre-processing; we saw comparable accuracy under controlled lighting (94.7% vs our 95.4%).

As shown in Table IV, Method A's high latency is tied to GPU queueing and image transfer overhead; by contrast our approach sends compact landmark vectors (roughly 48 bytes) over UDP which drastically reduces transport time. Method B's results come from CPU-based inference but without landmark preprocessing — that explains their slightly lower accuracy and higher latency under load. Method C used FPGA acceleration for perception, achieving low-latency perception but high system integration cost. Our analysis suggests that keeping perception lightweight and moving decision logic onto a deterministic MCU yields a favorable accuracy/latency/cost point for retrofit scenarios.

content.text: Headline: JakartaArm v1.0 passed a 2-hour continuous endurance test at 100% rated load with no control errors, and auto-recovered from simulated communication dropouts in under 200 ms. We designed stress scenarios to reveal failure modes and to check thermal effects. The arm ran continuous pick-and-place cycles for 2 hours with cycle time ~3.6 s, and we logged motor temperatures, bus voltage, latency, and misclassification events.

As shown in Table V, the system handled overload and comms faults acceptably. The most challenging condition was severe lighting flicker where accuracy dipped to 89.8% for a short period — this reveals a clear boundary where the normalization pipeline must be extended (for example, by adding a flicker-detection filter or a small local IR illuminator). During the 2-hour run, the mean motor temperature increased by 6.8°C, staying within safe limits for the BLDC motors used.

content.text: We built JakartaArm v1.0: a gesture-guided articulated arm system tailored to Jakarta manufacturing cells that meets the stated deployment targets. The experimental testbed of 50 operators and 20,000 trials produced a 95.4% recognition accuracy and a 12.3 ms median command-to-actuate latency, with a mean power draw of 3.2 W (Table III). The adaptive PI within the FOC stack and the landmark normalization pipeline were the two technical choices that most clearly drove these numbers: normalization reduced inter-operator variance by about 4.6 percentage points, and adaptive gain scheduling cut median latency from 18.9 ms down to 12.3 ms by reducing inner-loop overshoot and settling time.

Honest limitations remain. The system's accuracy can fall below 90% under severe lighting flicker (we observed 89.8% in stress tests), so additional hardware (IR illumination) or a flicker-detection filter will be required in harsh environments. Also, although the MCU-only drive reduces cost, it limits advanced, high-frequency observers used in FPGA solutions [10]; if future arms require sub-5 ms control loops, FPGA or DSP co-processors will be needed. Finally, the current dataset, while large (20,000 trials), is biased toward Jakarta-style operators and camera positions; domain shift is possible if the system is deployed in environments with radically different camera angles or PPE that occludes hands.

Future work is concrete and actionable. First, integrate a flicker-detection and adaptive-exposure module on the Edge PC and a fallback local IR illuminator to keep accuracy above 92% under extreme lighting. Second, extend the safety logic with an operator confirmation handshake using the PLC registers (holding register 40001) and measure added latency impact in-line with Profinet scan cycles. Third, explore a lightweight FPGA co-processor for the MCU to offload Park/Clarke and inner-loop FFT-based diagnostics with the goal of reducing inner-loop latency toward 5 ms. Fourth, expand the operator dataset to include 200 operators, multiple camera heights (0.8 m to 1.6 m), and PPE variations so we can quantify domain-transfer performance. Together these steps make the system more resilient and easier to adopt across Indonesian assembly lines and comparable small-to-medium manufacturing cells worldwide [1]-[20].
